strengths: Combining ten heterogeneous facial analysis tasks in one model is practically valuable and extends the coverage of the compared generalist systems.

The evaluation shows competitive results across several tasks: 3.52 MAE on BIWI, 3.05 NME on the full 300W set, and 91.83% attribute accuracy on CelebA. Cross-dataset results on 300VW also provide evidence of generalization, particularly on its challenging category.

Table 7 supports the usefulness of bidirectional attention: compared with standard cross-attention, head-pose MAE improves from 4.63 to 3.52 and landmark NME from 5.30 to 4.67. Backbone ablations and component-level computational profiling are useful additions.

The high-level architecture is understandable, and the appendix supplies substantial dataset and augmentation information. Acknowledging recognition tradeoffs and examining demographic disparities are positive aspects.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is insufficiently established. Task queries already appear in QFace and Faceptor, while the proposed self-attention, token-to-image attention, MLP, and image-to-token attention sequence closely resembles SAM's two-way decoder. SAM is cited as background, but this specific relationship is neither acknowledged nor differentiated. The strongest contribution currently appears to be integration and task coverage.

The central claim of simultaneous inference needs a reproducible common-input protocol. Section 3.4 motivates eliminating conflicting preprocessing, yet Appendices F.2 and F.7 use five-point alignment while F.3 uses loose crops. Section 4.2 also mentions three additional training epochs for unspecified tasks. These choices do not inherently invalidate unification, but the paper should establish that all reported results use one final checkpoint and a common inference pipeline.

Table 3 contains a consequential numerical inconsistency: the ten reported class scores average to 91.01, not 92.01. This reduces the advantage over Faceptor's 90.89 from 1.12 to 0.12 points. The correction does not erase competitive performance, but materially changes a highlighted result. Moreover, no quantitative race-prediction accuracy is provided despite race prediction being one of the ten claimed tasks.

Important training and evaluation details remain unresolved. Loss weights and treatment of missing task annotations are unspecified. Appendix F.5 introduces MORPH-II training and evaluation beyond the main dataset protocol without corresponding results. Exact splits and cross-task overlap handling also need documentation, particularly for related sources such as CelebA/CelebAMask-HQ and 300W/300W-LP.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed benefits of joint representation learning or explain why bidirectional attention enables a two-layer decoder. Matched single-task versus joint-training controls and decoder-depth comparisons are missing. Table 9 suggests a useful system-level efficiency tradeoff, but differing backbones and input resolutions prevent attributing the speed advantage specifically to FaceX; inference batch size, hardware, and preprocessing costs also need clarification.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Small benchmark improvements lack uncertainty estimates, and a handful of qualitative examples cannot establish broad robustness across ten tasks. The 'minimal bias' claim is particularly overstated: Table 8 reports an age disparity of 0.50, larger than CLIP's absolute 0.30 and FaRL's 0.35. Pooling six racial categories into one group can conceal disparities, and attributing fairness improvements to race co-training requires an ablation.
